recipe.history:
Scallions — also called green onions, spring onions, and Welsh onions — belong to the genus Allium, the great onion family that also encompasses garlic, leeks, chives, and shallots, and they are among the oldest cultivated plants in human history. Their origins are traced to Central Asia and the Far East, where wild Allium species have grown for thousands of years, and Chinese and Japanese cuisines developed the most sophisticated and varied uses of the scallion across their long culinary histories. In Japan, the negi — both thick leek-like varieties and slender bunching types — appears in everything from miso soup to yakitori to ramen, where charred green onion is sometimes run directly over an open flame before being sliced and scattered over the bowl. In Chinese cooking, scallions are one of the three aromatics — the holy trinity alongside ginger and garlic — foundational to the flavor building of the wok. The word 'scallion' itself derives from the Latin Ascalonia, suggesting an origin in Ashkelon, a port city in ancient Canaan on the Mediterranean coast of what is now Israel, though the taxonomic evidence points more convincingly to East Asia as the center of original domestication.

Scallions arrived in North America with both European settlers and Asian immigrants, and they took up residence in kitchen gardens and on restaurant tables across the continent. They were always a workmanlike garnish in American cooking — scattered over baked potatoes, chopped into cream cheese, added to stir fries — until grill culture and the charring movement of the late 2000s and 2010s transformed how American cooks thought about the onion family. Charring scallions whole over a high flame, as is done in the Mexican preparation of cebollitas alongside grilled meats, or in the Catalan calçots with their extraordinary romesco ritual, produces a result completely unlike raw scallion: the outer layers blacken and become slightly bitter and smoky, the interior turns sweet and almost creamy, and the flavor deepens from sharp and grassy to something rich and complex. Charred scallion butter and a scallion-sesame relish together make this burger a study in a single ingredient expressed at two very different temperatures and through two different techniques.

I grew up eating raw scallions whole, dipped in salt, as a snack — something I watched my great-uncle do as a child and adopted immediately because it seemed like the most adult possible thing a person could eat. The sharp green bite and the crunch of the white end, just barely kissed with salt, was a flavor I associated with seriousness and outdoor summer eating and confidence. Then a Korean barbecue restaurant showed me what scallions could be when you laid them whole across very high heat and left them there: the blackened, sweet, almost caramel-soft result was a revelation that restructured my understanding of the ingredient entirely. I have since become somewhat evangelical about charring scallions before using them in almost any context, including this burger, where the charred version goes into the butter and the fresh thinly sliced version goes into the relish, creating a before-and-after portrait of the same vegetable.

A burger cooked to medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — interacts with the charred scallion butter in a specific and important way: the warmth of the rested patty melts the butter slowly across its surface, so that each bite carries a trail of charred-scallion-inflected fat that floods the palate with smoke and sweetness simultaneously. The scallion-sesame relish adds cold brightness and crunch on top of that warmth. A well-done patty is a dry surface and the butter pools rather than melts into anything, and the relish sits on top of nothing interesting. Medium rare is the thermal condition under which this entire construction makes sense. It is not an opinion. It is a physical fact about how butter and beef interact at the right temperature.
ingredients: 2 large eggs (1 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 teaspoons toasted sesame seeds for topping
6 tablespoons unsalted butter, softened to room temperature
8 scallions, very thinly sliced (both white and green parts)
1/4 cup sesame oil (a blend of toasted and neutral if pure toasted sesame is too strong)
1 small clove garlic, minced to a paste
6 slices provolone or mild white cheddar (about 1 oz each)
instructions: 1. MAKE THE MILK BREAD BUNS: Combine warm milk, warm water, yeast, and 1 teaspoon of the sugar in a stand mixer bowl. Let stand 5 to 8 minutes until foamy.

2. Add bread flour, all-purpose flour, remaining sugar, salt, 1 egg, and butter. Mix on low with the dough hook 2 minutes, then increase to medium and knead 8 to 10 minutes until smooth, soft, and slightly tacky.

3. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 to 1 1/2 hours until doubled. Divide into 6 equal portions. Shape into tight round balls. Place on parchment-lined baking sheet and proof 45 minutes to 1 hour.
4. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Brush with egg wash (1 egg beaten with 1 tablespoon water). Sprinkle with toasted sesame seeds. Bake 14 to 16 minutes until golden. Cool completely on a wire rack.

5. MAKE THE CHARRED SCALLION BUTTER: Place whole scallions directly over a high gas flame, on a very hot cast-iron grill pan, or under a broiler. Char on all sides, turning occasionally with tongs, until the outer layers are blackened and the interior is soft and sweet, about 4 to 6 minutes. Cool slightly.

6. Peel and discard the blackened outer layers. Finely chop the softened charred interior. Combine with softened butter, soy sauce, sesame oil, black pepper, and a pinch of salt. Mix until thoroughly incorporated. Form into a log in plastic wrap and refrigerate until firm, at least 30 minutes. Can be made several days ahead.

7. MAKE THE SCALLION-SESAME RELISH: Combine thinly sliced raw scallions, both sesame seeds, rice wine vinegar, sesame oil, soy sauce, honey, red pepper flakes, and grated ginger in a small bowl. Toss to combine. Let sit at least 15 minutes for flavors to meld. Set aside.

8. MAKE THE GINGER-MISO AIOLI: Whisk egg yolks and mustard in a medium bowl. Whisk in garlic paste and ginger. Stream in neutral oil very slowly while whisking to form an emulsion. Stream in sesame oil blend. Whisk in miso paste and rice wine vinegar. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.
9. DRESS THE NAPA CABBAGE: Toss shredded napa cabbage with rice wine vinegar, sesame oil, and a pinch of salt just before assembly.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Gently combine ground chuck and ground short rib. Add soy sauce and sesame oil and mix in gently. Season with salt and pepper. Form into 6 patties, 4 1/2 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, with a center dimple. Refrigerate 20 minutes.
11. COOK THE PATTIES: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Cook patties without pressing, 3 minutes on the first side for a deep crust.

12. Flip once. Lay a slice of provolone or white cheddar over each patty. Cook 2 to 2 1/2 minutes more. Check internal temperature — target 130 to 135°F (54 to 57°C) for medium rare. Transfer to a wire rack.
13. Immediately top each patty with a generous pat — about 1 tablespoon — of charred scallion butter. Allow it to melt slowly over the warm patty as it rests for 3 minutes.
14. TOAST THE BUNS: Split buns and toast cut-side down in a hot dry skillet 60 to 90 seconds.
15. ASSEMBLE: Spread ginger-miso aioli generously on both cut sides of the bun. Place dressed napa cabbage on the bottom bun. Add the butter-basted, cheese-topped patty.
16. Spoon scallion-sesame relish generously over the patty. Finish with a pinch of flaky sea salt. Close with the top bun and serve immediately.
